analysis|07-29|1014|Η μάχη του Κλειδίου|The Battle of Kleidion|In the early eleventh century the Byzantine Empire was in a long conflict with the Bulgarian state of Tsar Samuel, which had extended its power over the Balkans. Basil II sought to restore Byzantine rule in the region. // Near Kleidion, on today's Greek-Bulgarian border, Basil II defeated the army of Samuel on 29 July 1014, in a battle with heavy losses for the Bulgarians. The victory placed Samuel in a difficult position and opened the way into Byzantine territory. // The emperor went down in history with the epithet "Bulgar-Slayer", and the Byzantine hold on the Balkans was strengthened for a time. The battle of Kleidion is known for the harsh treatment of prisoners and for its importance in Byzantine history. Basil II later established Byzantine administration in parts of Bulgaria, and his policy towards the Bulgarians was linked with the administrative organisation of Byzantium in the Balkans. The event is a subject of discussion for Byzantine and Bulgarian historiography. The site of the battle remains a point of reference for the discussion of Byzantine expansion in the Balkans.

analysis|07-29|1588|Η ναυμαχία του Γκραβελίν|The Battle of Gravelines|In the late sixteenth century Spain under Philip II was in rivalry with England under Elizabeth I, which supported the Dutch rebels and the Spanish opponents. Philip prepared a great campaign with the Armada to conquer England. // On 29 July 1588, in the Channel and near Gravelines in France, the English fleet attacked the Armada with fireships that broke up its formation. Spain did not manage to join the army of Parma, and the fleet was forced to begin its retreat. // The defeat of the Armada is regarded as a turning point in the conflict between the two countries, and the Spanish were forced to return northwards, with heavy losses from the storms. The English victory strengthened Elizabeth's prestige and opened the era of English naval supremacy. The defeat of the Armada gave England an advantage that strengthened its confidence at sea, and Spanish naval power gradually began to decline. The battle is often regarded as the beginning of English dominance of the oceans, which lasted for several centuries. The battle is regarded as a symbol of the naval technique of the age and continues to inspire historians and writers today.

analysis|07-29|1948|Οι Ολυμπιακοί Αγώνες του Λονδίνου|The London Olympic Games|After the Second World War Europe was in ruins, and the international sporting community decided to revive the Olympic Games. London, which had suffered bombing, undertook the organisation, although resources were limited. // The Games opened on 29 July 1948, twelve years after the Berlin Games of 1936, which had been interrupted by the war. The athletes were fewer than before, and Germany and Japan were not invited. // The London Games showed that international sport could return after the catastrophe, and they strengthened the sense of continuity of the Olympic movement. The event is regarded as an important step towards the reconstruction of post-war Europe. The organisation was carried out with modest means, and many athletes slept in barracks and schools, while the need for austerity was intense. The success of the Games contributed to the morale of the British and to the international reintegration of sports bodies after the war. The 1948 organisation is regarded as a milestone for the return of the Olympic movement after the war. The event contributed to the history of the Games with modest facilities, which later became a model for many cities.

analysis|07-29|1958|Ιδρύεται η NASA|NASA is founded|After the launch of Sputnik by the Soviet Union in 1957, the United States felt intense pressure in space technology and science. The need for a single state agency was now beyond dispute. // On 29 July 1958 President Eisenhower signed the law that founded the National Aeronautics and Space Administration, known as NASA. The new agency brought together existing activities and took over space planning. // NASA became the central body of American space research and led the great missions, such as the Apollo programme. Its founding marks the beginning of the organised American space effort, which continues to this day. The new agency gradually acquired a wider role, with Moon missions, satellites and research into the solar system. Its establishment became a turning point for American science, and its cooperation with universities and industries promoted technological progress. The agency continues to this day to organise space missions, with a strong presence in scientific research. The founding of the agency was linked with the history of the space rivalry, and its name is known throughout the world today.

analysis|07-29|1981|Ο γάμος του πρίγκιπα Καρόλου και της Νταϊάνα|The wedding of Prince Charles and Diana|In the early 1980s the British royal family was the subject of great public interest, and the heir to the throne, Prince Charles, was looking for a wife. The young Diana Spencer, of a noble family, became his choice and the theme of the age in the media. // On 29 July 1981 the ceremony took place at St Paul's Cathedral in London. The broadcast reached hundreds of millions of viewers across the world, and the event attracted great interest, with the bride's dress becoming a subject of discussion. // This marriage left a long legacy in the image of the British monarchy and in the relationship of its members with the public. The marriage later broke down, and the life and death of Diana continue to be discussed as a central chapter of modern British history. The marriage was accompanied by great celebrations in London and in other cities, and the public enthusiasm showed how strong the relationship of the public with the royal family still was. Subsequent changes in the life of the couple were followed with constant interest by the press and public opinion. The marriage remains a point of reference for modern British royal history and its cultural image.

analysis|07-30|1930|Ο πρώτος τελικός του Μουντιάλ|The First World Cup Final|The first football World Cup was held in 1930 in Uruguay, which was then the strongest football country of South America and had won the Olympic football tournaments of 1924 and 1928. European teams were few, because the journey was long and difficult. // In the final at Montevideo, on 30 July 1930, Uruguay beat Argentina 4–2 in front of a large crowd at the Centenario Stadium. The match was the first final of the competition, and Uruguay won the first world title in the history of the tournament. // The tournament laid the foundations for the World Cup, which became one of the most important sporting events in the world. The 1930 final remains the beginning of a competition that unites nations and peoples every four years. The competitive structure of the tournament, with groups and knockout stages, was established as a model for later editions. The final attracted a large crowd and became the first great moment of a competition that would unite peoples for more than a century. The final of 1930 is regarded as the beginning of a tournament that is followed today by the whole planet. That final remains a living part of the football memory of Uruguay.

analysis|07-30|1945|Βυθίζεται το καταδρομικό USS Indianapolis|The cruiser USS Indianapolis is sunk|In July 1945, towards the end of the Second World War, the American cruiser Indianapolis had carried the components of the atomic bomb to the base on the island of Tinian. The ship sailed without an escort in the Pacific, and its route had not been communicated to the appropriate authorities. // On 30 July 1945 the ship was struck by torpedoes from a Japanese submarine and sank within a few minutes. Of about 1,200 crew members, about 316 survived, who remained for days at sea without proper help, and many died from exposure, shark attacks and hunger. // The disaster remains in history as one of the worst naval tragedies of the United States, and it provoked debate about the responsibility of the command and about the way the survivors were sought. The episode continues to be studied by naval officers and historians. The delay in searching for the survivors was due to misunderstandings and an inability to communicate between the commands, and the case was the subject of investigations and legal proceedings. The history of the ship later became a work of art and a book, and it continues to be studied for the lessons it offers for the planning of operations.

analysis|07-31|1790|Εκδίδεται το πρώτο δίπλωμα ευρεσιτεχνίας των ΗΠΑ|The first US patent is issued|After the independence of the United States the new state needed a law that would protect inventions, in order to encourage innovation and technological progress. Congress passed the first patent law in 1790. // On 31 July 1790 the first American patent was issued to Samuel Hopkins, for a method of producing potash, a substance used in fertilisers and in industry. The patent was signed by President George Washington. // This patent laid the foundations of the American system for the protection of intellectual property, which contributed to the development of industry and technology. The first act is regarded as an important milestone for the American economy. The patent system became a basic tool of American industry, since it gave inventors the right to exploit their ideas. The law developed over the years, and its application contributed to the creation of many modern technologies. The first patent is today kept in archives and exhibitions that present the history of American innovation. The practice of patents helped the spread of inventions and the development of industry. The approval by the President of the country himself showed that the protection of inventions was regarded as a matter of national policy.

analysis|07-31|1964|Το Ranger 7 στέλνει φωτογραφίες της Σελήνης|Ranger 7 Sends Photographs of the Moon|In the early 1960s NASA was seeking information about the Moon before crewed missions, and the Ranger craft aimed to photograph the surface closely before impact. The first missions had failed, and the programme was still experimental. // On 31 July 1964 Ranger 7 sent back to Earth images of the Moon from short distance, before crashing on its surface. The photographs were among the first detailed images of the Moon and helped in the planning of the landing. // The success of Ranger 7 opened the way for the next craft of the programme, and the event was a basic step before the Apollo missions. The images first gave evidence about the surface and ground of the Moon. The photographs of Ranger 7 were among the first to show details of the lunar surface on a scale that had not been available until then. The data helped select the landing sites of later missions and the general understanding of the terrain the astronauts would meet. The Ranger missions contributed to the preparation of the crewed missions and remain a basic chapter of space history.

analysis|07-31|1991|Η συνθήκη START I|The START I Treaty|At the end of the 1980s the Cold War was beginning to recede, and the two superpowers were negotiating the limitation of strategic nuclear weapons. The negotiations for the START treaty had begun in 1982, with difficulties over limits and verification. // On 31 July 1991 the United States and the Soviet Union signed the START I treaty in Moscow, which provided for the reduction of strategic nuclear weapons and for an inspection system. It was the first agreement to provide real reduction and verifiable control. // The treaty formed the basis for later arms control agreements, and the Cold War ended shortly afterwards with the dissolution of the Soviet Union. START I is regarded as a milestone for international security and nuclear deterrence. The agreement set limits on the number of nuclear warheads and delivery systems, and established verification arrangements that allowed inspection of the installations. The implementation of the treaty contributed to greater trust between the two superpowers at a critical period of transition. The treaty was the starting point for a series of new agreements, which contributed to the reduction of the number of nuclear weapons.

analysis|08-01|1914|Η Γερμανία κηρύσσει πόλεμο στη Ρωσία|Germany declares war on Russia|After Austria-Hungary's clash with Serbia, Russia had begun mobilisation in support of Serbia, and Germany regarded this action as a threat. The alliances of the period had made the conflict almost inevitable. // On 1 August 1914 Germany declared war on Russia, and the conflict spread to the eastern front. A few days later Germany invaded Belgium and France, and the war spread across the whole of Europe. // The war spread across the whole continent within a few days, and the fronts that were opened remained for years. The conflict changed the political, social and military structures of Europe for decades. The German declaration of war came after diplomatic attempts that failed to prevent the conflict, and the military logic of the plans of the period accelerated the developments. The war on the eastern front became one of the most bloody theatres of the conflict. The 1st of August is remembered as the day the eastern front officially opened. This decision remains one of the most critical of the war, since it opened a huge front that would require very great resources.

analysis|08-01|1944|Αρχίζει η Εξέγερση της Βαρσοβίας|The Warsaw Uprising Begins|In 1944 Poland was under German occupation, and the Home Army of the internal resistance was waiting for the opportunity to liberate the capital before the arrival of the Soviet army. The Soviet army had reached near Warsaw, and the resistance hoped for an alliance. // On 1 August 1944 the Home Army rose against the Germans, but the reinforcement from the Soviet army did not come. The battles lasted sixty-three days, with enormous destruction and with hundreds of thousands of civilians killed or expelled. // The uprising ended with capitulation and the almost complete destruction of the city. The sacrifice of the people of Warsaw remains a symbol of Polish resistance, and the city was rebuilt after the war. The uprising had a great moral impact and showed the determination of the Poles to claim their freedom, even with limited means. The silence of the Soviet forces on the outskirts of the city was a subject of discussion about the political intentions of Stalin. The uprising remains today a point of reference for the memory of the Polish struggle and is commemorated every year in the city. The uprising left behind a deep political and historical debate about the role of the Soviet leadership.

analysis|08-01|1960|Ανεξαρτησία του Μπενίν|Independence of Benin|In the late 1950s the French colony of Dahomey, in West Africa, sought its independence, as did other colonies on the continent. France had begun to grant autonomy to many regions of Africa, and independence became gradually a matter for negotiation. // On 1 August 1960 Dahomey became an independent country, and in 1975 it was renamed Benin. Independence was granted after negotiations with France, and the new government took over the administration of the country. // Independence opened the way for self-government in Benin, but the country later experienced political instability and military coups. The modern course of the country is linked with efforts for democracy and development. Independence was granted within a wider framework of decolonisation in West Africa, and the new government inherited institutions and language from the colonial period. The political developments that followed showed the difficulties that new states face in organising administration. The day of independence is a national festival and recalls the long path of the country towards self-government. The day of independence is linked with the change of the country's name, which took place in 1975.

analysis|08-01|1981|Ξεκινά το MTV|MTV Launches|In the early 1980s the music industry was closely linked with the music video, and television had begun to be the main means of promoting artists. New television channels sought to meet this need. // On 1 August 1981 MTV began its broadcasts in the United States, with the first video clip being "Video Killed the Radio Star" by The Buggles. The channel was devoted exclusively to music with video, which became a new form of pop culture. // MTV changed the relationship of the public with music and influenced fashion, cinema and advertising. The channel became a global phenomenon and is regarded as the starting point of modern music television. The channel became a model for other music television programmes, and the form of the music video influenced the way artists create and promote their music. Its influence appeared in television advertising and in the design of today's digital platforms. The channel remains today a point of reference for the relationship of music with the visual culture of the media. The broadcast of the first clips marked the beginning of an era in which the image became an integral part of music.

analysis|08-02|-216|Η μάχη των Καννών|The Battle of Cannae|In the third century BC Carthage and Rome were contesting control of the western Mediterranean in the Second Punic War. Hannibal, the Carthaginian general, had crossed the Alps with his army and had defeated the Romans in earlier battles in Italy. // Near Cannae in Apulia, in the spring of 216 BC, Hannibal arranged his army in a way that trapped the Roman legions. The centre of his army deliberately gave way, and the Roman legions entered the formation, while Hannibal's flanks encircled them. The battle ended in catastrophe for Rome. // The victory of Cannae is regarded as one of the greatest military achievements of antiquity and is still studied as a model of encirclement. However, Hannibal did not manage to take Rome, and the war later ended in favour of the Romans with Scipio's victory. The encirclement at Cannae became a subject of study for generals of all periods, and it is often cited as an example of effective tactics. Hannibal's victory, however, did not lead to the surrender of Rome, since the city managed to gather new armies and continue the war.

analysis|08-02|1934|Πεθαίνει ο Χίντενμπουργκ|Hindenburg Dies|In 1933 Hindenburg, president of the German Republic and hero of the First World War, had appointed Hitler chancellor, hoping to control his government. Hitler, however, quickly strengthened his power, and Hindenburg had remained politically weak. // On 2 August 1934 Hindenburg died on his estate, at the age of 86. A few hours later a law was announced uniting the offices of president and chancellor, and Hitler now assumed full power. // The army accepted the change, and the officers' oath now became personal to Hitler. The union of the offices gave the Nazi regime its final form and opened the way to the war that followed. The president's death gave Hitler the opportunity to combine power and to demand an oath of loyalty from the army to his person. The change was decisive for the consolidation of the Nazi regime and for Germany's course towards war. This period is studied today as decisive for Germany's transition to the Nazi regime. The death of the president did not provoke great reaction, since Hitler already controlled the mechanisms of the state.

analysis|08-02|1990|Το Ιράκ εισβάλλει στο Κουβέιτ|Iraq invades Kuwait|At the end of the 1980s Iraq, under Saddam Hussein, was in economic crisis after the war with Iran. Iraq accused Kuwait of drawing oil from the Rumaila fields and of reducing oil prices. // On 2 August 1990 the Iraqi army invaded Kuwait and quickly occupied the country. The invasion was condemned by the UN, which imposed an embargo and eventually authorised military action for its liberation. // The crisis led to the First Gulf War, with a coalition of many states under the United States, which liberated Kuwait in February 1991. The conflict changed the balance in the region and left a legacy that affected the following decades. The international reaction was immediate, and the Security Council condemned the invasion and imposed a trade embargo on Iraq. The crisis showed how important oil was for the world economy, and it affected the strategies of the great powers in the region for many years. The international alliance that followed contributed to the liberation of Kuwait, but the region remained sensitive for years.

analysis|08-03|1492|Ο Κολόμβος ξεκινά το πρώτο του ταξίδι|Columbus begins his first voyage|At the end of the fifteenth century the Spain of the Catholic Monarchs had completed the Reconquista, and Christopher Columbus proposed a voyage westward to reach Asia. The proposal was dangerous, but the Spanish court financed it with an agreement that included titles and trading rights. // On 3 August 1492 Columbus left the port of Palos in Spain with three ships, the Santa Maria, the Pinta and the Niña. The expedition crossed the Atlantic and reached the Bahamas and the Caribbean, and Columbus believed he had reached India. // The voyage opened European presence in America, with consequences that profoundly changed both continents. Columbus's arrival, on 12 October, is regarded as the beginning of an era of great exchanges, but also of serious disasters for the indigenous peoples. The expedition had a strong scientific and commercial dimension, since Columbus believed that the Earth was smaller than most thought, and he wanted to find an easier route to Asia. The arrival in America changed the geographical map and brought with it deep social and economic consequences. The departure point at Palos remains a place of memory of Spanish naval history.

analysis|08-03|1914|Η Γερμανία κηρύσσει πόλεμο στη Γαλλία|Germany Declares War on France|After declaring war on Russia, Germany had applied the Schlieffen Plan, which envisaged a quick victory over France before the full mobilisation of Russia. To apply the plan, the German army had to pass through neutral Belgium. // On 3 August 1914 Germany declared war on France, and the First World War now spread across the whole of Europe. The decision made the conflict large and multi-front. // The war in the West soon became a war of trenches, with huge losses and fronts that remained almost static for years. The declaration of war remained in history as the beginning of a conflict that changed Europe. The declaration of war on France followed the German invasion of Luxembourg, and German strategy rested on the idea of a lightning campaign. The failure of the quick victory led to years of trench warfare on the Western Front. The 3rd of August remains in history as the day of the extension of the war to Western Europe. The entry of German troops into Belgium was the cause of the British reaction. This decision came a few days after the declaration of war on Russia, in an environment where the mobilisation of the great powers had already begun.

analysis|08-03|1960|Ανεξαρτησία του Νίγηρα|Independence of Niger|At the end of the 1950s the French colony of Niger, in West Africa, sought its autonomy. France, in a general policy of decolonisation in Africa, agreed to grant independence to its colonies in the region. // On 3 August 1960 Niger became an independent country, with Hamani Diori as its first president. Independence was recognised by France, and the new government took over the administration of the country with successive reforms. // Independence opened the way for a state with challenges in development, education and economic relations with France. Niger later experienced political changes and military coups, and the day of independence remains a national festival. Niger's independence came in a wave of similar decisions for the colonies of West Africa, and the new leaders sought a balance between tradition and development. The country later faced challenges in the economy and in the security of its borders. The day of independence is celebrated in the country as a national festival, with ceremonies and rituals. The new country was later involved in international negotiations on development and on the security of its borders.

analysis|08-04|1789|Καταργείται η φεουδαρχία|Feudalism Is Abolished|At the end of 1788 and the beginning of 1789 French society was deeply divided between the privileges of the clergy and the nobles and the Third Estate. Agrarian uprisings had intensified, and the National Assembly was seeking a solution to the social crisis. // At the night session of 4 August 1789 the National Assembly voted the abolition of feudal privileges, through which the nobles and the clergy had special rights and taxes. The decision was taken almost in one night and with enthusiasm. // The vote opened the way to the new legal equality of citizens, which was recorded later in the Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen. The night is regarded as one of the critical points of the Revolution and of the modern history of Europe. The decision opened the way for the Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen, which was voted a few weeks later. The abolition of privileges was part of a wider restructuring of society, which determined the politics of Europe for the next century. The night of 4 August is regarded today as a symbol of the abolition of privileges in France. The abolition of privileges was the first step towards changing the agrarian relations and abolishing the tithes.

analysis|08-04|1914|Η Βρετανία κηρύσσει πόλεμο στη Γερμανία|Britain declares war on Germany|Britain had traditionally had an interest in not allowing a single power to dominate continental Europe, and it had agreed to guarantee the neutrality of Belgium. The German invasion of Belgium, a neutral state, created strong reaction in London. // On 4 August 1914 Britain declared war on Germany, after an ultimatum that went unanswered. Britain's entry gave the conflict a worldwide dimension, since its empire was involved in all the oceans. // British participation brought huge losses and a strong military effort on the Western Front and on other fronts. The decision was decisive for the course of the war and for the shaping of postwar Europe. Britain's entry gave the war an international dimension, since it secured the participation of the empire and its colonies. Its participation on the Western Front and at sea affected the strategies of both sides throughout the war. 4 August remains as the date that connects Britain with the First World War. The decision turned the conflict into a world war, with the participation of all the British colonies. The government supported the conflict on the grounds of protecting Belgium and maintaining the balance of power in Europe.

analysis|08-04|1944|Συλλαμβάνεται η οικογένεια της Άννας Φρανκ|Anne Frank's Family Is Arrested|During the German occupation of the Netherlands, the Frank family, of Jewish origin, had hidden for two years in a secret apartment behind an office building in Amsterdam. The members of the family had help from Dutch friends, who supplied them with food and news. // On 4 August 1944 the Germans and their Dutch collaborators discovered the hidden apartment, and the members of the family were arrested and sent to concentration camps. Anne, the younger daughter, died at Bergen-Belsen a few months later. // Anne Frank's diary, which survived, became one of the best-known texts of the Holocaust and has been translated into many languages. The text remains as testimony to human dignity in the barbarity of war. The arrest followed a denunciation, and the members of the family were transported to concentration camps, where many of them did not survive. The case of the family is one of the most moving testimonies to the fate of the Jews of Europe during the Second World War. The house in Amsterdam is today a museum, which attracts visitors from all over the world. The story of the family has been researched in many books and documentaries, which record the persecution of the Jews in the Netherlands.

analysis|08-04|2020|Η έκρηξη στο λιμάνι της Βηρυτού|The Beirut port explosion|In the 2010s Lebanon's economic crisis had reached a deep form, and corruption and lack of governance were intense. In the port of Beirut large quantities of ammonium nitrate, a dangerous chemical, had been stored for years without suitable precautions. // On 4 August 2020 a huge explosion took place in the port warehouses, with about 220 people killed and thousands injured. The explosion was recorded from a great distance and destroyed much of the city, with damage to houses, hospitals and buildings. // The tragedy caused great anger among the people and led to the resignation of the government. Investigations into responsibility continued for years, and the disaster remains a symbol of corruption and of the need for transparency in the public sector. The explosion caused enormous destruction at a great distance from the port, and thousands of people were left homeless. International organisations offered help, and local volunteers mobilised, and the event highlighted the importance of safety in storing dangerous materials. 4 August is commemorated as a day of remembrance for the victims and their families. The explosion led to international investigations into responsibility and to demonstrations for transparency in public administration.

analysis|08-05|1960|Ανεξαρτησία της Άνω Βόλτα|Independence of Upper Volta|The area that today is called Burkina Faso was a French colony under the name Upper Volta. After the Second World War the African colonies of France acquired greater autonomy, and in the late 1950s independence became a real demand of local leaders. // On 5 August 1960 the country became independent, and France recognised its independence. The new government took over administration, with political forces that wanted to organise the state on the basis of the needs of the inhabitants. // Independence opened the way for a state with challenges in development, education and political stability. The country changed its name in 1984 to Burkina Faso, and the day of independence remains important in its collective memory. The independence of the country was accompanied by the organisation of the first governmental institutions and by negotiations for economic cooperation with France. The country still faces challenges in development and security today, which are related to the history of the colonial period. The name of the country was changed to Burkina Faso, and the day of independence remains important in its collective memory. Independence led to the first national elections and to the formation of a distinct national identity.

analysis|08-05|1962|Πεθαίνει η Μέριλιν Μονρόε|Marilyn Monroe dies|In the early 1960s Marilyn Monroe was the best-known actress of Hollywood, with a great career in cinema and an intense public presence. Her life was full of pressures from publicity and from the media, and her personal difficulties were well known. // On 5 August 1962 Monroe was found dead in her home in Los Angeles, at the age of 36. Her death was attributed to an overdose of drugs, according to the official investigations, although the case continued to be discussed for years. // The actress became a symbol of the Hollywood age and of its public image, and her name is associated with one of the most famous images of American culture. Her life and death continue to inspire books, films and discussions about the culture of fame. Her life and death have been the subject of countless documentaries and books, which try to understand her fame and the problems of her private life. Her image remains in the culture of the twentieth century and is associated with the mythology of American cinema.

analysis|08-05|1962|Συλλαμβάνεται ο Νέλσον Μαντέλα|Nelson Mandela is arrested|South Africa in the 1960s lived under the apartheid regime, with legal distinctions between white and black citizens. The African National Congress had begun to resort to forms of armed resistance, after the ban on peaceful demonstrations. // On 5 August 1962 Nelson Mandela, leader of the ANC, was arrested near Durban, and was later sentenced to imprisonment. Mandela had already spent a considerable time underground and in international publicity as a symbol of resistance. // His imprisonment lasted almost three decades, and Mandela became an international symbol of freedom and reconciliation. When he was released in 1990, he led South Africa's transition to democracy, and later became its first black president. The arrest was followed by a long trial in which Mandela defended the positions of the ANC, and his speech became one of the most important texts of the era. His time in prison became a symbol of resistance to the regime, and international pressure for his release grew continually. The 5th of August remains in history as the day when the long imprisonment of the fighter began.

analysis|08-05|1963|Η Συνθήκη Μερικής Απαγόρευσης Πυρηνικών Δοκιμών|The Partial Nuclear Test Ban Treaty|After the 1950s atmospheric nuclear tests had caused concern about radioactivity and the spread of pollution across the planet. The Cuban missile crisis of 1962 had also shown the danger of a nuclear war. // On 5 August 1963 the United States, the Soviet Union and Britain signed the Partial Test Ban Treaty, which forbade nuclear tests in the atmosphere, in outer space and under water. The signatures were made in Moscow, and the remaining tests were permitted underground. // The treaty was an important step towards limiting nuclear tests and reducing radioactive pollution. It formed a basis for later arms control agreements and is regarded as a milestone of the international effort for stability. The treaty did not ban underground tests, but it marked a first agreement between the superpowers on limiting nuclear weapons. The cooperation required for the treaty opened the way for later negotiations on arms control. The treaty began a series of agreements for the control of nuclear arms. It was signed in Moscow, and its provisions are still cited as a basic step in the history of disarmament.

analysis|08-06|1806|Τέλος της Αγίας Ρωμαϊκής Αυτοκρατορίας|End of the Holy Roman Empire|The Holy Roman Empire had for centuries been a loose collection of German states and cities, with a common emperor but without a strong central power. In the early nineteenth century Napoleon had created the Confederation of the Rhine, which strengthened his influence over the German lands. // On 6 August 1806 Francis II resigned the title of emperor of the Romans, while keeping the title of emperor of Austria, and the empire was formally dissolved. The decision was the result of French pressure and of Napoleon's victorious progress. // The dissolution ended a long history that had begun in the tenth century. It opened the way for the new German political synthesis of the nineteenth century, and the idea of unity of the Germans developed in the following years. The dissolution left behind many independent states, which would later form the German Confederation. The history of the empire is linked with the long tradition of power in Europe, and its dissolution became a landmark in German political history. The day of the dissolution is cited today as a milestone of European history. The dissolution of the empire was linked with the treaties of the Napoleonic era and with the creation of new state formations.

analysis|08-06|1825|Ανεξαρτησία της Βολιβίας|Independence of Bolivia|In the early nineteenth century Bolivia, which was part of the Spanish colonial empire, experienced strong independence movements after the revolution in South America. The leaders of the struggle, with Simón Bolívar and Antonio José de Sucre, claimed liberation from Spain. // On 6 August 1825 the congress of the region's representatives proclaimed its independence from Spain. The country took the name Bolivia in honour of Bolívar, and Sucre later took charge of the administrative affairs of the new republic. // Independence did not immediately bring stability, since the country experienced political unrest and wars with its neighbours, such as the War of the Pacific. The day of independence remains a national festival, and the event is regarded as a basic element of the country's history. The new republic bore the name of Bolívar, and the history of the country in the following years was marked by efforts to build institutions.
